strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching failure with a simple, training-free module: identify problematic seam regions, refine their alignment, and reconnect local seams. Its compatibility with existing pipelines offers useful practical value.

Tables 1–2 report consistent improvements across 79 image pairs, four seam-cutting methods, and five alignment methods, including UDIS++. For example, baseline SSIM on SEAGULL improves from 0.638 to 0.697 with REW alignment.

The visual examples demonstrate repairs to structural discontinuities. The parameter ablations and explicit small-patch failure discussion help characterize the method. The pipeline and pseudocode are understandable, underlying methods and public datasets are cited, and a code repository is linked.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation does not adequately establish overall mosaic quality. All four metrics compare patches around the selected seam and can miss distortions or discontinuities introduced elsewhere. Table 3 demonstrates this directly: removing the sigmoid improves RMSE, SSIM, and ZNCC on all three datasets despite introducing boundary artifacts. Consequently, the central alignment-versus-boundary-quality tradeoff needs independent assessment of the resulting mosaics, such as systematic perceptual comparisons or measurements of structural distortion.

The originality and comparative advantage are insufficiently established. The implementation combines established SSIM/Otsu detection, SIFT flow, sigmoid weighting, and constrained graph cuts. The modular refinement design is useful, but the broader paradigm claims need clearer differentiation from seam-guided alignment [22] and dense-matching-based seam/warp estimation [35]. Parallax and SEAGULL receive selected qualitative comparisons rather than dataset-wide quality and runtime comparisons; adding LPAM to UDIS++ alignment also does not establish an advantage over complete competing stitching systems.

The seam acceptance rule contradicts the broad claim of dissociating quality from initial alignment. Section 3.2 accepts a seam whenever max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q), which also accepts uniformly high-error seams and performs no repair. This dependence on errors being localized is not characterized experimentally, and the assertion that false-positive repairs cannot worsen results is unsupported.

The claimed boundary consistency is not guaranteed by the formulation. At beta = 8, the sigmoid endpoints are approximately 0.018 and 0.982, and weighting along one coordinate does not generally constrain all patch boundaries. Fixing boundary labels preserves label assignments but does not ensure continuity of warped image content. The acknowledged failure case makes this practically relevant. Repair-rectangle padding, overlapping-patch handling, and out-of-patch sampling are also insufficiently specified for reproducing this behavior.

The efficiency claim needs qualification. Section 4.4 reports LPAM time separately from host seam cutting: on SEAGULL, the baseline takes 4.11 seconds and LPAM adds 7.34 seconds. This establishes a substantial additional cost, without a comparison against complete alternative pipelines. Image resolutions, detailed SIFT-flow settings, and acquisition/preprocessing details for the new dataset are also missing from the supplied manuscript, limiting reproducibility.
